## The idea

Networks grow. New websites link to existing ones, new papers cite old ones, newcomers to a city make friends. Who do they connect to? Often to whoever is already well connected, which is preferential attachment, and partly to whoever is good: the most useful website, the best paper, the most interesting person. Page's formation model combines the two: a newcomer links to existing nodes in proportion to their degree plus their quality.

The balance between the two decides who becomes a hub. When quality varies little, the network is pure preferential attachment and the hubs are simply the oldest nodes, whose head start compounds. When quality has a long tail, a brilliant latecomer can overtake the incumbents. The model lets us ask how much of a node's prominence reflects merit and how much reflects timing.

## Formulation

::: {.model-box}
**Setup.** Start with $d$ disconnected nodes. Each period $t$, a new node arrives with quality $Q_t$ drawn from a distribution $F$, and links to $d$ distinct existing nodes.

**Rule.** With $D_{it}$ the degree of node $i$ at time $t$, the new node links to node $i$ with probability

$$
\Pr(i) = \frac{D_{it} + Q_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} \big(D_{jt} + Q_{j}\big)} .
$$

**Result.** With low-mean, low-variance quality, the model is preferential attachment: a long-tailed degree distribution whose hubs are the earliest nodes. With a long-tailed quality distribution, high-quality late arrivals can become hubs.
:::

We draw quality from a lognormal distribution with a chosen mean and spread; the book leaves $F$ general.

## Interactive model

Three hundred nodes arrive one at a time, each linking to two existing nodes. Each dot is a node: its arrival time against its final degree, coloured by quality. With little quality variation, degree falls steadily with arrival time: the first movers win. Increase the quality spread and the hubs become the high-quality nodes, whenever they arrived.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, cor, C, fmt} from "../js/models.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof meanQ = Inputs.range([0.1, 10], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Mean quality"})
viewof spreadQ = Inputs.range([0, 2.5], {value: 0.2, step: 0.1, label: "Quality spread (lognormal sd)"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 17, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
formation = {
  const r = rng(seed), N = 300, d = 2;
  const drawQ = () => meanQ * Math.exp(r.normal(-spreadQ * spreadQ / 2, spreadQ));
  const deg = [], Q = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < d; i++) { deg.push(0); Q.push(drawQ()); }
  for (let t = d; t < N; t++) {
    const w = deg.map((k, i) => k + Q[i]), chosen = new Set();
    while (chosen.size < d) chosen.add(r.weighted(w));
    for (const i of chosen) deg[i]++;
    deg.push(d); Q.push(drawQ());
  }
  const nodes = deg.map((k, i) => ({i, arrival: i + 1, degree: k, quality: Q[i]}));
  const top = nodes.slice().sort((a, b) => b.degree - a.degree).slice(0, 10);
  return {
    nodes, top,
    corAge: cor(nodes.map(n => -n.arrival), nodes.map(n => n.degree)),
    corQ: cor(nodes.map(n => Math.log(n.quality)), nodes.map(n => n.degree))
  };
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "Quality and Degree Network Formation: arrival time against final degree",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: arrival order of each node. Vertical axis: its final degree, on a log scale. Dots are coloured by quality from light (low) to dark (high). The summary below the chart states the result in words.",
  height: 300,
  x: {label: "Arrival order"},
  y: {label: "Final degree", type: "log", grid: true},
  color: {type: "log", scheme: "viridis", label: "Quality", legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(formation.nodes, {x: "arrival", y: "degree", fill: "quality", r: 3.5, stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 0.2})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const early = formation.top.filter(d => d.arrival <= 30).length;
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`The best-connected node has **${formation.top[0].degree}** links; the median node has ${d3.median(formation.nodes, d => d.degree)}. Degree correlates **${fmt(formation.corAge, 2)}** with earliness of arrival and **${fmt(formation.corQ, 2)}** with (log) quality. ${early} of the 10 biggest hubs arrived among the first 30 nodes. ${formation.corQ > formation.corAge ? "Here quality, not timing, decides who becomes a hub." : "Here timing beats quality: early arrivals' head start compounds."}`}</div>`;
}
```

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# Quality and degree network formation.
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(igraph))
n <- 300
d <- 2 # links made by each new node
mean_q <- 1
spread_q <- 0.2 # lognormal sd of quality
set.seed(17)

draw_q <- function() mean_q * exp(rnorm(1, -spread_q^2 / 2, spread_q))
deg <- rep(0, d)
q <- replicate(d, draw_q())
edges <- c()
for (t in (d + 1):n) {
  chosen <- sample.int(t - 1, d, prob = deg + q) # degree plus quality
  deg[chosen] <- deg[chosen] + 1
  deg <- c(deg, d)
  q <- c(q, draw_q())
  edges <- c(edges, rbind(t, chosen))
}
g <- make_graph(edges, n = n, directed = FALSE)

cat(sprintf(
  "Largest degree %d; cor(degree, earliness) %.2f; cor(degree, log q) %.2f\n",
  max(degree(g)), cor(degree(g), -(1:n)), cor(degree(g), log(q))
))
plot(1:n, degree(g),
  log = "y", pch = 19,
  col = hcl.colors(10)[cut(log(q), 10)], xlab = "Arrival order",
  ylab = "Final degree"
)
```

## Takeaways

::: takeaways
- Linking in proportion to degree makes the rich get richer and produces hubs.
- Adding quality to the attachment rule lets merit compete with incumbency; how much depends on the spread of quality.
- The same long-tailed network can arise from luck and timing or from differences in quality, so structure alone cannot tell us which.
:::

## Uses

::: uses
- **Explain.** Why the most-cited papers and most-linked websites are often old, and when newcomers break through.
- **Reason.** Separate the roles of first-mover advantage and quality in markets with network effects.
- **Predict.** Forecast which nodes will become hubs from their age and early growth.
:::
